messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Fashion Designer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 41

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me, Avoid Dreams: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares, Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Marcus

Marcus was fifty-five when he finally came to see a therapist, though the wounds that brought him there had been open since childhood. He had spent the first twelve years of his life in a household where his father's rage was as unpredictable as it was brutal—not the kind of violence that announced itself, but the kind that lived in silence. A wrong word at dinner, a shirt left on the floor, the simple fact of existing in his father's line of sight on a bad day: any of these could trigger a beating that left Marcus gasping, certain he was about to die. What made it worse was the silence that preceded it—those long, suffocating minutes when his father would go quiet, and Marcus would know something terrible was coming but not when or how hard. He learned to read the stillness in a room the way other children learned to read a clock.

By his twenties, Marcus had built a life that seemed to keep those memories at bay. Fashion design gave him a world of color and texture, of creation and control. But the trauma had never actually left; it had only learned to hide. In his mid-forties, after his divorce, the symptoms began to crystallize. Marcus had come to believe that he was fundamentally broken, that something essential in him had been destroyed by those early years. This conviction had seeped into everything. He was certain that people could not be trusted—that beneath every friendly gesture lay the potential for betrayal—and this belief drove him to withdraw from colleagues and friends, to work longer hours alone in his studio, to ruminate bitterly about perceived slights and old wounds. The more he dwelled on what others had done to him, the more his negative appraisals about himself deepened, feeding a vicious spiral: he was damaged, people were dangerous, and his isolation was the only logical response.

The threat he felt was no longer confined to his father's presence. It had generalized into the texture of his everyday life. At home in his loft, even with the doors locked, Marcus remained vigilant, hyperalert to any sound that might signal danger. Unusual silence—the kind that filled his apartment on quiet evenings—triggered an almost unbearable sense of dread, as though something catastrophic was about to unfold. When a colleague or friend approached him unexpectedly, even with good intentions, his body would jolt with alarm before his mind could catch up. These startle responses terrified him. He had begun to wonder if he was losing his grip on reality, if his mind was fragmenting. The fear that he was going crazy had become as present as the fear of violence itself.

His memories of the abuse remained fragmented and emotionally strange. When he tried to piece together a coherent account of what had happened—to explain it to himself or, more recently, to a therapist—the narrative dissolved. There were images, sensations, the smell of his father's cologne mixed with sweat, the sound of a belt being unbuckled, but no continuous story that made sense. More unsettling still was the way he could sometimes recall specific incidents in vivid detail yet feel absolutely nothing, as though he were watching a film about someone else's suffering. At other times, memory brought a crushing wave of guilt—not guilt about anything he had done, but a deeper, more irrational conviction that he had somehow deserved the violence, that he must have done something fundamentally wrong to provoke it. This guilt was inseparable from his sense that he was permanently damaged, that the abuse had rewritten him at some cellular level.

The rumination had become his constant companion. Marcus would lie awake cataloging his failures—moments he had mishandled at work, relationships he had sabotaged, the ways he had let people down. He also cycled obsessively through his father's cruelties, replaying scenes, imagining different outcomes, as though if he could just think about it hard enough, understand it deeply enough, he could change what had happened or at least make sense of it. But the more he ruminated, the more fragmented his memories became, and the more he questioned his own perception of reality. His therapist had gently suggested that his constant self-blame and his dwelling on others' betrayals were keeping him trapped, that they were preventing his mind from integrating what had happened into a coherent narrative. Yet stopping felt impossible. The rumination was a kind of compulsion, a way of trying to regain control in a mind and body that felt fundamentally unsafe.

Marcus had begun avoiding the times of day when nightmares were most likely—the early mornings when he would wake gasping—by staying up late, working obsessively on designs until exhaustion forced sleep. But this had left him depleted and even more isolated. He had not been on a date in three years. His professional relationships, once warm, had cooled to cordial distance. What frightened him most now was not just the trauma itself, but the possibility that he had become irredeemably changed by it, that he was incapable of trust or genuine connection, and that his mind was fragmenting under the weight of all he could not remember and could not forget. He had come to therapy hoping for some kind of repair, though he was not entirely sure such a thing was possible.
